s: female beauty and obesity is produced by forced feeding (for girls before marriage)
q: They then swallow three times a day regular boluses of paste, and are not allowed to take exercise.

s: early marriage includes marriage at age nine (among girls in Mogador)
q: whilst the merchants were at Morocco, a little girl of nine years of age was married to a man upwards of fifty.

s: early marriage is common at ages ten and eleven (for girls)
q: Ten and eleven is a common age for girls to be married.

s: marriage customs treat marriage as sale and barter (among Jewish and Moorish communities)
q: Indeed, nearly all marriages here are matters of sale and barter.

s: Jewish polygamy permits four wives (under privilege granted in Mahometan countries)
q: The Jews, at times, though but very rarely, avail themselves of their privilege of four wives granted them in Mahometan countries

s: Mogador Jewesses attend balls (in European society)
q: The European Jewesses settled in Mogador, are indeed the belles of society, and attend all the balls (such as they are).

s: white brandy is consumed by Moorish subjects (under the claim that it is not grape juice)
q: Moors drink it under protest, that it is not the juice of the grape.

s: Dr. Brown attends Muley Abd Errahman (as a physician)
q: When Dr. Brown was attending the Sultan

s: Moorish court has anecdotes related about Muley Abd Errahman
q: Friend Cohen came in one afternoon, and related several anecdotes of the Maroquine Court.

s: France can assist Moroccan Jews (through governmental action)
q: The Governments of France and England can do much for them in Morocco.

s: England can assist Moroccan Jews (through governmental action)
q: The Governments of France and England can do much for them in Morocco.

s: Mogador Jewesses are exempt from walking barefoot in the streets (by imperial privilege)
q: For such reasons, Jewesses are now privileged and exempted from the painful necessity of walking barefoot in the streets.

s: Moroccan Jews improve in manners (after entering European society)
q: Monsieur Delaport, Consul of France, was the first official person who brought prominently forward the native and other Jews into the European society of this place, and since then, these Jews have improved in their manners, and increased their respectability.

s: Moroccan Jews increase in respectability (after entering European society)
q: Monsieur Delaport, Consul of France, was the first official person who brought prominently forward the native and other Jews into the European society of this place, and since then, these Jews have improved in their manners, and increased their respectability.

s: European merchants come from Gibraltar (among the principal places of origin)
q: The principal European Jews are from London, Gibraltar, and Marseilles.

s: European merchants come from Marseilles (among the principal places of origin)
q: The principal European Jews are from London, Gibraltar, and Marseilles.

s: Shereefs is a dynasty (descended from the Prophet; regal and sacerdotal)
q: The Shereefs, though descended from the Prophet, are not strictly priests, or, to make the distinction perfectly clear the Shereefs are to be considered a dynasty corresponding to the type of Melchizdek, uniting in themselves the regal and sacerdotal authority

s: Islam roots out notions of human sacrifice (from the human mind)
q: If the Mahometan religion has been powerful in any one thing, it is in that of rooting out from the mind of man every notion of human sacrifice.

s: Graeberg de Hemso is consul-general (for Sweden and Sardinia at Morocco)
q: Graeberg de Hemso, whilst consul-general for Sweden and Sardinia (at Morocco!)

s: Yezeed is a tyrant (Moroccan ruler)
q: Here the daughter of Erin brought forth this ferocious tyrant

s: Yezeed is descended from Sidi Mohammed (son)
q: who boasted of having within its sacred enclosure of love and bliss, a woman from every clime. Here the daughter of Erin brought forth this ferocious tyrant

s: Yezeed is partly descended from Ireland (through his renegade Irish maternal line)
q: Yezeed was half-Irish, born of the renegade widow of an Irish sergeant of the corps of Sappers and Miners

s: Yezeed advocates carnage (as a principle of government)
q: whose maxim of carnage, and of inflicting suffering on humanity was, "My empire can never be well governed, unless a stream of blood flows from the gate of the palace to the gate of the city."

s: Yezeed makes war on the world (except the English)
q: To do Yezeed justice, he followed out the instincts of his birth, and made war on all the world except the English (or Irish).

s: Shereefs are jealous of Moravedi (because the Shereefs once possessed the throne)
q: On account, of their once possessing the throne, the Shereefs have a peculiar jealousy of Marabouts, and which latter have not forgotten their once being sovereigns of Morocco.

s: Yezeed is associated with Tully's Letters on Tripoli (for accounts of his exploits)
q: Tully's Letters on Tripoli give a graphic account of the exploits of Yezeed

s: European consuls make obeisance to Yezeed (as son of the Shereef enthroned in the West)
q: Meanwhile, our European consuls made profound obeisance to this son of the Shereef, enthroned in the West.

s: Barbary is also called land of Barbary (a hostile derivation attributed to De Haedo de la Captividad)
q: I have accustomed myself to call that land the land of Barbary.

s: Moors derives from their dark complexions (according to the Greeks)
q: In Latin, Mauri, Maurice, Maurici, Maurusci, and it is supposed, so called by the Greeks from their dark complexions.

s: Berbers include Berber race (a principal or present Moroccan grouping)
q: In Morocco, there are Amayeegh and Shelouh

s: Berbers include Kabyles (a present Algerian grouping)
q: in Algeria the Kabyles

s: Berbers include Aoures (a present Tunisian grouping)
q: in Tunis the Aoures, sometimes the Shouwiah

s: Shereefs are not priests (strictly)
q: The Shereefs, though descended from the Prophet, are not strictly priests

s: Atlantic System is a mountain system (covering the heights of the Maghreb and elevations of the Sahara)
q: Of the 'Systeme Atlantique,' which derives its name from the Mount Atlas, renowned for so many centuries, and still so little known; we include in this vast system, all the heights of the region of Maghreb--we mean the mountain of the Barbary States--as well as the elevations scattered in the immense Sahara or Desert.

s: Atlas Mountains extend from Cape Noun (toward the east of the Great Syrte)
q: It appears that the most important ridge extends from the neighbourhood of Cape Noun, or the Atlantic, as far as the east of the Great Syrte in the State of Tripoli.

s: Atlas Mountains cross Morocco (as part of the principal ridge)
q: In this vast space it crosses the new State of Sidi-Hesdham, the Empire of Morocco, the former State of Algiers, as well as the State of Tripoli and the Regency of Tunis.

s: Atlas Mountains have greatest heights in Morocco (especially east of the town of Morocco and southeast of Fez)
q: It is in the Empire of Morocco, and especially in the east of the town of Morocco, and in the south-east of Fez, that that ridge presents the greatest heights of the whole system.

s: Sahara contains elevations of the Atlantic System (scattered throughout the desert)
q: we include in this vast system, all the heights of the region of Maghreb--we mean the mountain of the Barbary States--as well as the elevations scattered in the immense Sahara or Desert.

s: Tangier is a garrison our old garrison
q: we must again possess ourselves of our old garrison of Tangier.

s: Fez is a capital of the realm of Fez (western royal court according to cited authorities)
q: Fes or sea Fez, the capital of the realm of that name

s: Fez is ancient city (already ancient before the Mohammed Anuabi of the Muslims)
q: Fez was already a very ancient city before the Mohammed Anuabi of the Mussulmen

s: Moravedi is a family of priests (formerly sovereigns of Morocco)
q: whilst the _Marabouteen_ were a family of priests like the sons of Aaron.

s: Yezeed is a son of the Shereef (as recognized by European consuls)
q: Meanwhile, our European consuls made profound obeisance to this son of the Shereef, enthroned in the West.

s: Moravedi have been sovereigns of Morocco (formerly)
q: which latter have not forgotten their once being sovereigns of Morocco.

s: Abd-el-Kader unites princely and sacerdotal authority (like the Shereefs; not of the Prophet's family)
q: Abd-el-Kader unites in himself the princely and sacerdotal authority like the Shereefs, though not of the family of the Prophet.

s: human sacrifice is rejected by Moors (throughout Barbary)
q: First of all, the sacrifice of human beings is repudiated by every class of inhabitants in Barbary.

s: Morocco is a independent Mussulman kingdom (in North Africa)
q: Morocco is the only independent Mussulman kingdom remaining, founded by the Saracens when they conquered North Africa.

s: Shereefs are venerated by Islam (by true Mussulmen)
q: I have not heard that there is anywhere a dynasty of Shereefs except in this country. They are, therefore, profoundly venerated by all true Mussulmen.

s: Shereefs succeeds the Arabian Sovereigns of Spain
q: The Shereefian Sultans of Morocco are not only the successors of the Arabian Sovereigns of Spain, but may justly dispute the Caliphat with the Osmanlis, or Turkish Sultans.

s: Muley Abd Errahman is a Shereefian prince (reigning prince)
q: 36. Muley Abd Errahman, nephew of Muley Suleiman and eldest son of Muley Hisham, the reigning Shereefian prince.

s: Muley Abd Errahman is nominated by Muley Suleiman (to the throne)
q: Muley Abd Errahman was nominated to the throne by the solemn and dying request of his uncle, Muley Suleiman, to the detriment of his own children.

s: Muley Abd Errahman is son of Muley Hisham (eldest son)
q: 36. Muley Abd Errahman, nephew of Muley Suleiman and eldest son of Muley Hisham, the reigning Shereefian prince.

s: Muley Abd Errahman is nephew of Muley Suleiman (familial relationship)
q: 36. Muley Abd Errahman, nephew of Muley Suleiman and eldest son of Muley Hisham, the reigning Shereefian prince.

s: Muley Abd Errahman is a man of middle stature (personal appearance)
q: His Moorish Majesty, who is advanced in life, is a man of middle stature.

s: Muley Abd Errahman has dark and expressive eyes (personal appearance)
q: He has dark and expressive eyes, and, as already observed, is a mulatto of a fifth caste.

s: Muley Abd Errahman is mulatto of a fifth caste (personal appearance)
q: He has dark and expressive eyes, and, as already observed, is a mulatto of a fifth caste.

s: Muley Abd Errahman uses Imperial parasol (sole visible emblem distinguishing him from officers and governors)
q: This Emperor is so simple in his habits and dress, that he can only be distinguished from his officers and governors of provinces by the _thall_, or parasol, the Shereefian emblem of royalty.

s: Muley Abd Errahman is not given to excesses (generally)
q: Muley Abd Errahman is not given to excesses of any kind, (unless avarice is so considered), though his three harems of Fas, Miknas, and Morocco may be _stocked_, or more politely, adorned, with a thousand ladies or so, and the treasures of the empire are at his disposal.

s: Muley Abd Errahman has three harems (at Fas, Miknas, and Morocco)
q: Muley Abd Errahman is not given to excesses of any kind, (unless avarice is so considered), though his three harems of Fas, Miknas, and Morocco may be _stocked_, or more politely, adorned, with a thousand ladies or so, and the treasures of the empire are at his disposal.

s: Muley Abd Errahman is not man of blood (rarely decapitates ministers or governors)
q: He is not a man of blood; [4] he rarely decapitates a minister or a governor, notwithstanding that he frequently confiscates their property, and sometimes imprisons them to discover their treasures, and drain them of their last farthing.

s: Muley Abd Errahman has son Sidi Mohammed (governor of Fez)
q: He has one son, Governor of Fez (Sidi Mohammed), and another son, Governor of Rabat.

s: Muley Abd Errahman has son Governor of Rabat (son and governor of Rabat)
q: He has one son, Governor of Fez (Sidi Mohammed), and another son, Governor of Rabat.

s: Muley Suleiman is uncle of Muley Abd Errahman (paternal or dynastic uncle)
q: Muley Abd Errahman was nominated to the throne by the solemn and dying request of his uncle, Muley Suleiman, to the detriment of his own children.

s: Muley Hisham is father of Muley Abd Errahman (eldest son)
q: 36. Muley Abd Errahman, nephew of Muley Suleiman and eldest son of Muley Hisham, the reigning Shereefian prince.

s: Tafilett is inhabited by Shereefs (small fortified town inhabited entirely by them)
q: This state of things is happily past, and, as to the number of the Shereefs at Tafilett, all that we know is, there is a small fortified town, inhabited entirely by Shereefs, living in moderate, if not impoverished circumstances.

s: Abd-el-Kader is a marabout warrior (revered throughout North Africa)
q: Abd-el-Kader is a marabout warrior, greatly revered and idolized by all enthusiastic Mussulmen throughout North Africa, more especially in Morocco, the _terre classique_ of holy-fighting men; but though the Maroquines were disaffected, groaning under the avarice of their Shereefian Lord, and occasionally do revolt, nevertheless they would not deliberately set aside the dynasty of the Shereefs, the veritable root and branch of the Prophet of God, for an adventurer of other blood, however powerful in arms and in sanctity.

s: Morocco contains Tafilett (ancient country of the Shereefs)
q: The greater part of the royal family reside at Tafilett, the ancient country of the _Sherfah_, or Shereefs, and is still especially appropriated for their residence.

s: Abd-el-Kader does not dethrone Shereefian dynasty (despite military power and sanctity)
q: It was a great error to suppose that Abd-el-Kader could have succeeded in dethroning the Emperor during the hostilities of the Emir against the lineal representative of the Prophet.

s: Edristees has capital Fez (founded by Edrio)
q: 1st. The Edristees (pure Saracens,) their capital was Fez, founded by their great progenitor, Edrio.

s: Moravedi is a Marabout dynasty (rose to consequence about 1050)
q: 4th. Moravedi (or Marabouteen,) that is to say, Marabouts, [2] who rose into consequence about 1050, and their first prince was Aberbekr Omer El Lamethounx, a native of Sous. Their dynasty terminated in 1149.

s: Morocco is ruled by Shereefian dynasty (present dynasty)
q: 8th. The Shereefs (Oulad Ali) of the present dynasty, whose founder was Hasein, have now occupied the Imperial throne more than three centuries.

s: Fatima is a daughter of Islam (only daughter)
q: 1. Ali-Ben-Abou-Thaleb; died in 661 of the Christian Era; surnamed "The accepted of God," of the most ancient tribe of Hashem, and husband of Fatima, styled Ey-Zarah, or, "The Pearl," only daughter of Mahomet.

s: Abdullah-el-Kamel is father of Muley Edris (progenitor of the Edristi dynasty)
q: 4. Abdullah-el-Kamel, _i.e._ "The Perfect;" in 752, father of Edris, the progenitor or founder of the dynasty of the Edristi in Morocco, and who had six brothers.

s: Maroquine dynasties terminate in Shereefian dynasty (historical succession)
q: Morocco, an immense and unwieldly remnant of the monarchies formed by the Saracens, or first Arabian conquerors of Africa, has had a series of dynasties terminating in that of the Shereefs.

s: Muley Edris founds Edristees (dynasty in Morocco)
q: 4. Abdullah-el-Kamel, _i.e._ "The Perfect;" in 752, father of Edris, the progenitor or founder of the dynasty of the Edristi in Morocco, and who had six brothers.

s: Muley Abdullah is succeeded by Sidi Mohammed (genealogical succession)
q: 31. Muley Abdullah, in 1757. 32. Sidi Mohammed, in 1789.

s: Sidi Mohammed is succeeded by Yezeed (genealogical succession)
q: 32. Sidi Mohammed, in 1789. 33. Muley Yezeed, who assumed the surname of El-Mahdee _i.e._ "the director," in 1792.

s: Yezeed is succeeded by Muley Hisham (genealogical succession)
q: 33. Muley Yezeed, who assumed the surname of El-Mahdee _i.e._ "the director," in 1792. 34. Muley Hisham, in 1794.

s: Muley Hisham is succeeded by Muley Suleiman (genealogical succession)
q: 34. Muley Hisham, in 1794. 35. Muley Suleiman, in 1822.

s: Shereefian dynasty is a dynasty (reigning dynasty of Morocco)
q: 8th. The Shereefs (Oulad Ali) of the present dynasty, whose founder was Hasein, have now occupied the Imperial throne more than three centuries.

s: Imperial parasol honors Sidi Mohammed (when on military expedition)
q: The Emperor's son, when out on a military expedition, is also honoured by the presence of the Imperial parasol, which was found in Sidi Mohammed's tent at the Battle of Isly.

s: Algeria is integral portion of France (under the Republic)
q: Algeria has now become an integral portion of France by the Republic.

s: Tunis is a regency of the Port of Tunis (has an hereditary Bey)
q: Tunis and Tripoli are regencies of the Port of Tunis, having an hereditary Bey, while Tripoli is a simple Pasha, removable at pleasure.

s: Shereefian dynasty originates in Medina (family origin)
q: This family of Shereefs came from the neighbourhood of Medina in Arabia, and succeeded to the empire of Morocco by a series of usurpations.

s: Shereefian dynasty has branch Hoseinee Shereefs (first branch)
q: They are divided into two branches, the Sherfah Hoseinee, so named from the founder of the dynasty, who began to reign at Taroudant and Morocco in 1524, and over all the empire in 1550, and the Sherfah El Fileli, or Tafilett, whose ancestor was Muley Shereef Ben Ali-el-Hoseinee, and assumed sovereign power at Tafilett in 1648, from which country he extended his authority over all the provinces of that empire.

s: Shereefian dynasty has branch Fileli Shereefs (second branch)
q: They are divided into two branches, the Sherfah Hoseinee, so named from the founder of the dynasty, who began to reign at Taroudant and Morocco in 1524, and over all the empire in 1550, and the Sherfah El Fileli, or Tafilett, whose ancestor was Muley Shereef Ben Ali-el-Hoseinee, and assumed sovereign power at Tafilett in 1648, from which country he extended his authority over all the provinces of that empire.

s: Muley Hisham is a Sultan (proclaimed in Morrocco and Sous)
q: Muley Hisham, who was proclaimed Sultan in the south at Morrocco and Sous

s: Muley Hisham retires to sanctuary (in 1795)
q: In 1795, Hisham retired to a sanctuary where he soon died

s: Muley Suleiman is a Emperor (proclaimed in the north at Fez)
q: Muley Suleiman, who was saluted as Emperor in the north at Fez.

s: Muley Suleiman is a good and patriotic prince
q: Muley Suleiman proved to be a good and patriotic prince, "the Shereef of Shereefs,"

s: Muley Suleiman's reign lasts for a quarter of a century (approximately)
q: During his long reign of a quarter of a century, at a period when all the Christian powers were convulsed with war, he wisely remained neutral

s: Muley Suleiman remains neutral neutral
q: he wisely remained neutral, and his subjects were happy in the enjoyment of peace and prosperity.

s: Muley Suleiman dies on 28 March 1820 (about the 50th year of his age)
q: He died on the 28th March 1820, about the 50th year of his age

s: Muley Suleiman declares successor Muley Abd Errahman (his nephew and the legitimate hereditary successor)
q: with his last breath declared his nephew, Muley Abd Errahman, the legitimate and hereditary successor of the Shereefs

s: Muley Suleiman abolishes Christian slavery (in his States; described as his most beneficent act toward European nations)
q: the abolition of Christian slavery in his States.

s: abolition of Christian slavery is a act of Muley Suleiman (described as the most glorious and beneficent act of his reign for Europeans)
q: The most glorious as well as the most beneficent and acceptable act of the reign of Muley Suleiman, so far as European nations were concerned, was the abolition of Christian slavery in his States.

s: Shereefian lineage omits names Yezeed
q: we miss the names of the two brothers, the Princes Yezeed and Hisham

s: Muley Abd Errahman pursues the most pacific policy (by the assistance of his new vizier, Bouseilam)
q: the latest account from this most interesting Moorish country, represents Muley Abd Errahman as steadily pursuing, by the assistance of his new vizier, Bouseilam, the most pacific policy.

s: France establishes relations with Morocco (shortly after England; French flags appeared at Moroccan ports in 1555)
q: The French entered regularly into relations with the western Moors shortly after us; their flag, indeed, began to appear at their ports in 1555, under Francis I.

s: England occupies Tangier (during the period of Anglo-Moorish struggles)
q: They succeeded in gaining the favour of the Moors whilst we occupied Tangier

s: Yezeed is a hereditary prince (son of Sidi Mohammed)
q: although Yezeed was the hereditary prince, and succeeded his father three days after his death

s: peace of Utrecht cedes Gibraltar (to England)
q: after the peace of Utrecht, conceding Gibraltar to England

s: British influence in Morocco becomes supreme after Trafalgar (following the fall of Napoleon)
q: the battle of Trafalgar, and the fall of Napoleon, established the supremacy of British influence over the minds of the Shereefs

s: slave trade is justified by Islam (in the Sultan's correspondence with Mr. Hay)
q: As regards the making of slaves and trading therewith, it is confirmed by our book, as also of the _Sunnat_ (or traditions) of our Prophet.

s: Islam permits slave trade (according to the Shereefian correspondence and cited religious authorities)
q: As regards the making of slaves and trading therewith, it is confirmed by our book, as also of the _Sunnat_ (or traditions) of our Prophet.

s: Moorish law shall not go before Kady or Hakem (as the Consul's decision shall suffice)
q: the English subject shall not go before the Kady or Hakem, as the Consul's decision shall suffice.

s: British-Moroccan treaties include Treaty of Fez of 1801 (signed at Fez on 14 June 1801)
q: All, however, of any value, are embodied in the treaty between Great Britain and Morocco, signed at Fez, 14th June 1801

s: Article VII provides for British subjects (disputes with Moorish subjects are decided in the presence of English consuls, subject to Moorish law)
q: "VII. Disputes between Moorish subjects and English subjects, shall be decided in the presence of the English Consuls, provided the decision be comformable to the Moorish law

s: Yezeed is a Sultan (proclaimed at Salee after Sidi Mohammed's death)
q: being proclaimed Sultan at Salee with accustomed pomp and magnificence

s: British subjects has no real security no real security for British subjects in this country
q: there can be no real security for British subjects in this country

s: Mogador has governor the Governor of Mogador
q: A few months before my arrival in that place, this gentleman was adjudged, in the presence of his Consul, Mr. Willshire, and the Governor of Mogador

s: Mr. Willshire is a Consul (present during Mr. Saferty's adjudication at Mogador)
q: this gentleman was adjudged, in the presence of his Consul, Mr. Willshire, and the Governor of Mogador

s: Yezeed is a tyrant (described by the author as exceptionally cruel)
q: Yezeed--the tyrant whose bad fame and detestable cruelties filled with horror all the North African world.

s: Yezeed dies on February 1792 (after being mortally wounded by a poisoned arrow; stated as the 22nd month of his reign)
q: was mortally wounded by a poisoned arrow, shot from a secret hand, and died in February 1792, the 22nd month of his reign, and 44th year of his age.

s: Yezeed is buried at Kobah Sherfah (with great solemnities)
q: he was interred with great solemnities at the mosque of _Kobah Sherfah_ (tombs of the Shereefs)

s: Yezeed's succession crisis is a civil war (following Yezeed's death)
q: A civil war still followed this monster's death, and the empire was rent and partitioned into three portions

s: Muley Hisham is a pretender (to the Shereefian throne; proclaimed in the south)
q: The two grand competitors, however, were Muley Hisham, who was proclaimed Sultan in the south at Morrocco and Sous

s: Empire of Morocco has population about six million (proximate amount)
q: The proximate amount of this population is six millions.

s: Empire of Morocco includes Tafilett (eastern province with nominal or distant authority)
q: finally, Tafilett and the provinces on the eastern side of the Atlas, are too remote to feel the influence of the central government.

s: Empire of Morocco claims sovereignty over Touat (authority now purely nominal)
q: they still claim sovereignty over the oases of Touat, a month's journey in the Sahara.

s: Empire of Morocco claims sovereignty over Western Sahara (former claim extending toward Timbuctoo)
q: The Shereefs once pretended to exercise authority over all Western Sahara as far as Timbuctoo

s: Empire of Morocco has native name El-Gharb (meaning The West)
q: Maroquine Moors call their country El-Gharb, "The West,"

s: Empire of Morocco has native name Mogrel-el-Aksa (meaning The far West)
q: and sometimes Mogrel-el-Aksa, that is "The far West:"

s: Empire of Morocco has native name Blad Muley Abd Errahman (meaning Country of the Sultan Muley Abd Errahman)
q: Among the Moors generally, Morocco is now often called, "Blad Muley Abd Errahman", or "Country of the Sultan Muley Abd Errahman."

s: Morocco is bounded by Mediterranean Sea (to the north)
q: The Maroquine Empire, with its present limits, is bounded on the north by the Mediterranean Sea and the Straits of Gibraltar

s: Morocco is bounded by Algeria (to the east)
q: on the east by Algeria, the Atlas, and Tafilett

s: Morocco is situated between latitudes 28° and 40° N. Latitude
q: and the whole is situate between the 28 deg. and 40 deg. N. Latitude.

s: Sultan of Morocco exercises authority over Sous (no real power)
q: Over the provinces of the south, Sous and Wadnoun, the Sultan has no real power

s: Sultan of Morocco exercises authority over Wadnoun (nominal acknowledgment and occasional presents)
q: The countries of Sidi, Hashem, and Wadnoun nominally acknowledge the Emperor, and occasionally send a present

s: Sultan of Morocco is more firmly established than Sultan of the Ottomans (according to the favorable assessment)
q: The Sultan is the head of the orthodox religion of the Mussulmen of the West, and more firmly established on his throne than the Sultan of the Ottomans.

s: Sultan of Morocco has influence over Western Barbary (as a sovereign Shereef)
q: His influence, as a sovereign Shereef, spreads throughout Western Barbary and Central Africa, wherever there is a Mussulman to be found.

s: Sultan of Morocco has influence over Central Africa (wherever Muslims are found)
q: His influence, as a sovereign Shereef, spreads throughout Western Barbary and Central Africa, wherever there is a Mussulman to be found.

s: North Africa has indigenous population Berbers (aboriginal inhabitants)
q: When the Romans, a century and a half before Christ, received, or wrested, the rule of Africa from the Phoenicians, or Carthaginians, they found before them an indigenous people, whom they indifferently called Moors, Berbers, or Barbarians.

s: North Africa was invaded by Phoenicians (successive invasions and establishment on the coast)
q: But the most ancient historical fact on which we can depend is, the invasion, or more properly, the successive invasions of North Africa by the Phoenicians.

s: North Africa was conquered by Romans (after Carthaginian rule)
q: When the Romans, a century and a half before Christ, received, or wrested, the rule of Africa from the Phoenicians, or Carthaginians

s: North Africa was conquered by Vandals (Romans were subjugated for about a century)
q: Some ages later, the Romans, too weak to resist a vigorous invasion of other conquerors, were subjugated by the Vandals, who, during a century, held possession of North Africa

s: North Africa was conquered by Arabs (from the middle of the seventh century)
q: Towards the middle of the seventh century after Christ, and a few years after the death of Mahomet, the Romans, in the decline of their power, had to meet the shock of the victorious arms of the Arabians, who poured in upon them triumphant from the East

s: Empire of Morocco has religious head Sultan of Morocco (the Sultan is head of the orthodox religion of Western Muslims)
q: The Sultan is the head of the orthodox religion of the Mussulmen of the West

s: Berbers are also called Moors (in Roman usage)
q: But the Romans likewise called the aboriginal tribes of North Africa, Moors, or Mauri

s: Berbers are also called Barbarians (in Roman usage)
q: whom they indifferently called Moors, Berbers, or Barbarians.

s: Berbers is located in the mountains (mostly)
q: Maroquine Berbers, include the varieties of the Amayeegh [14] and the Shelouh, who mostly are located in the mountains

s: Arabs inhabit North Africa (introduced through conquest and later migrations)
q: The Arabs who invaded Northern Africa about 650, were all natives of Asia

s: Arabs invaded North Africa (around 650)
q: The Arabs who invaded Northern Africa about 650, were all natives of Asia

s: Arabs invaded Spain (in the first years of the eighth century)
